title: Barkin sees interest rate hikes ahead, but at a gradual pace
description: In a CNBC interview, the policymaker expressed concern over inflation and said monetary policy will need to adjust.
content: Barkin sees interest rate hikes ahead, but at a gradual pace Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond President Thomas Barkin attends a conversation with the Economic Club of Washington DC in Washington, D.C., U.S., April 9, 2025. Kevin Mohatt | Reuters Richmond Federal Reserve President Thomas Barkin said Thursday that he expects the central bank will have to raise interest rates further, though he's not sure by how much or at what pace. In a CNBC interview that was part of the Richmond Fed's 2026 CFO Summit, the policymaker expressed concern over inflation and said monetary policy will need to adjust. "Unemployment's near record lows, and inflation is too high. That means the path is pretty straightforward. The question, of course, is pace," Barkin said in the talk with CNBC's Steve Liesman. "Gradual makes sense if you think there's uncertainty in the world, and if you think that there's information you're going to get in the period. And I think that's still a pace that makes sense to me," he added. Barkin's comments come a little more than a week after his colleagues voted to keep the Fed's benchmark overnight borrowing rate anchored in a range between 3.75% and 4%. While Barkin is not a voting member on the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee now, he will be in 2027. In its post-meeting statement, the FOMC said that it is awaiting the "accumulation of more information" as it deliberates where to go next. When the committee OK'd a quarter percentage point hike in September, officials largely agreed that another increase was likely before the end of 2026. Barkin said he considers current policy close to a point where it neither restricts nor promotes growth, which officials consider a neutral rate. "If you're restricting the economy, presumably you're restricting consumption, which is you know roughly two thirds of the economy, and that's relatively elevated," he said. "So that would make the case that we're a little bit accommodative somewhere in that place." Inflation, he added, "is the most important risk right now ... and I hope that our move in September and whatever else we might choose to do in the future will have some impact on inflation," he added. Artificial intelligence is one source of price pressures, though he said it eventually will spur production and help ease inflation farther down the road. Markets are pricing in a better than 80% chance of a hike in December, then one more move in 2027, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. This is breaking news. Please refresh for updates .
